title: Spot the Vulnerability
blurb: Real .NET code, one flaw each. Find the vulnerable line, then pick the fix a security reviewer would actually accept.

levels.title: L1 · The user search
levels.prompt: Which line is the vulnerability, and what's the fix? (Injection · A05)

payload.intro: An ASP.NET Core controller action searching users by name.

nodes.label: var sql = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '" + name + "'";

fixes.label: Wrap the query in a try/catch

levels.explain: Concatenating untrusted input into SQL lets an attacker inject their own SQL. FromSqlInterpolated (or FromSqlRaw with real parameters) sends the value separately from the query text, so it can never be executed as code.

failStates.title: The execution isn't the bug
failStates.explain: FromSqlRaw is fine when given a parameterized query. The vulnerability is the line that BUILDS the SQL by concatenating untrusted input.

failStates.title: Encoding is for XSS, not SQL
failStates.explain: HTML-encoding protects HTML output. For SQL, the fix is parameterization — keep the value out of the query text entirely.

failStates.title: A try/catch hides errors, not the hole
failStates.explain: Catching exceptions doesn't stop the injection — the malicious query still runs. Parameterize the query.

levels.title: L2 · The order lookup
levels.prompt: Every user is authenticated. Which line is the flaw, and the fix? (Broken Access Control · A01)

payload.intro: An endpoint that returns an order by id. [Authorize] is already on the controller.

fixes.label: Scope to the owner: load where order.UserId == currentUserId, else 404/403
Use a Guid id so it can't be guessed

levels.explain: Find(id) returns ANY order, so an authenticated user can read someone else's by changing the id (IDOR). The fix is an ownership check — load the order only if it belongs to the current user. This is authorization on the specific resource, not just being logged in.

failStates.title: [Authorize] isn't enough
failStates.explain: The user is already authenticated — [Authorize] only confirms they're logged in. It does nothing to stop them reading another user's order. You must check that THIS order belongs to THIS user.

failStates.title: Unguessable ids aren't access control
failStates.explain: Swapping int for Guid is security through obscurity — ids leak in URLs, logs, and referrers. The real fix is an ownership check on every access.

failStates.title: The route isn't the problem
failStates.explain: Exposing an id in the route is normal. The flaw is that the lookup never verifies the caller owns that order.

levels.title: L3 · Storing a password
levels.prompt: Which line is the flaw, and the fix? (Cryptographic Failures · A04)

payload.intro: How the app hashes a new user's password before saving it.

fixes.label: Use a slow, salted password hash — Identity's PasswordHasher (PBKDF2), or bcrypt/Argon2

levels.explain: MD5 is fast and unsalted — attackers brute-force billions of guesses per second and rainbow-table the rest. Passwords need a deliberately SLOW, salted hash: ASP.NET Core Identity's PasswordHasher (PBKDF2), or bcrypt/Argon2.

failStates.title: SHA-256 is still too fast
failStates.explain: SHA-256 is stronger than MD5 for integrity, but it's still a FAST general-purpose hash — an attacker can try billions per second. Password storage needs a slow, salted algorithm (PBKDF2/bcrypt/Argon2), not just a 'stronger' fast hash.

failStates.title: Base64 isn't hashing
failStates.explain: Base64 is reversible encoding — anyone can decode it back to the password instantly. That's strictly worse.

failStates.title: Storing the hash is fine
failStates.explain: Persisting a hash is normal — the flaw is WHICH hash. MD5 is the wrong algorithm for passwords.
